title: For its own sake (Avot 6:1)
hook: whoever learns for its own sake gains much and is called a friend
tomorrow: what do you owe someone who taught you one tiny thing?

segments.voice: Yesterday, according to the effort: the reward follows what it cost, not the scoreboard. Today, the last chapter of Avot opens.

The email starts with thank you for your interest, and everyone knows how the next sentence goes. After a no like that, a real question shows up. If the answer is no, why keep doing the thing at all? Avot's sixth chapter opens with an answer in one Hebrew word: lishmah. For its own sake.
screen: `THANK YOU FOR YOUR INTEREST.` → `IF THE ANSWER IS NO…` → `LISHMAH.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Meir says: whoever studies Torah lishmah, for its own sake, gains many things, and the whole world is worth it for that person. They're called a friend, beloved, one who loves God and loves all creatures. Here's the question under it: what does for its own sake mean, if the mishnah then lists rewards? The answer seems to be that these are things that come only when you stop chasing them. Study for the grade and you get a grade. Study for the thing itself and you may end up a friend of God and of people, which no one can hand you. The Talmud adds a kindness: start anyway, even for the wrong reasons, because from not for its own sake comes for its own sake. Now a neighbor who says something close. In the Bhagavad Gita, a Hindu scripture, Krishna tells the warrior Arjuna that his right is to the action alone, never to its fruits; don't let the fruit be your motive. Two traditions, one shared insight: the work done for itself, without clutching at what it earns. And an honest difference. The Gita speaks of action and duty on a battlefield, and asks to let go of the fruit entirely. Avot speaks of learning Torah, and still names what comes: a friend, beloved, a lover of God and of all creatures. Each says it in its own words.
screen: `LISHMAH: FOR ITS OWN SAKE.` · `WHAT COMES WHEN YOU STOP CHASING.` · `THE GITA: THE ACTION, NOT THE FRUIT.` · `SHARED, AND STILL DIFFERENT.` · then, large: `FOR ITS OWN SAKE.`

segments.voice: Listen to one sound around you: a fan, traffic, a bird, your own breath. Don't use it for anything; don't name it, don't try to relax with it. Just listen to it for its own sake, until the bell.
screen: `ONE SOUND.` · `DON'T USE IT FOR ANYTHING.` · `JUST LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Lishmah: for its own sake. Rabbi Meir's word for learning done for itself, which turns out to be when the most comes.
Keep this close: for its own sake, and let the rest come to you unchased. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1483 COUNTS.` → `AVOT, CHAPTERS 3–6 · 56 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: WHAT DO YOU OWE SOMEONE WHO TAUGHT YOU ONE TINY THING?`

howItsDone: The ideal of Torah lishmah, learning for its own sake, runs through Jewish study; chapter six of Avot, which opens with Rabbi Meir's saying, is read on the last summer Shabbat afternoons of the Avot cycle.

notes: Avot 6:1 paraphrased: Rabbi Meir: whoever engages in Torah lishmah merits many things; the whole world is worthwhile for his sake; he is called friend, beloved, loves the Omnipresent, loves the creatures. Chapter six is a baraita (Kinyan Torah) appended to Avot; the script says only 'Avot's sixth chapter'. Confirm.
Pesachim 50b (Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav): one should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for from not for its own sake comes for its own sake. Confirm.

UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): shared with Hinduism: Bhagavad Gita 2:47, paraphrased (not quoted; no certain public-domain wording): your right is to the action alone, never to its fruits; let not the fruit be your motive. Honest difference: the Gita on action and duty, letting go of the fruit entirely; Avot on Torah learning, and still naming what comes. No ranking; neither said to be 'the same'. A Hindu Keeper should confirm the Gita summary.
